lesson.text: Quick memory: what are the five steps of the design cycle? (Idea, plan, make, test, improve.) Today: designing products that use electricity, like a torch or an alarm.
Electricity flows round a complete loop called a circuit: from the battery, along the wires, through the bulb and back to the battery. Make a gap anywhere in the loop, and it stops.
A switch is a gap you can open and close. Closed, the loop is complete and the bulb lights. Open, the loop is broken and the bulb goes out.
Many products are a circuit inside a case. A torch: a battery, a switch and a bulb. A fan: a battery, a switch and a motor. An alarm: a battery, a switch and a buzzer.

Switches come in many kinds: push switches, slide switches and pressure pads. A pressure pad is like two pieces of foil with sponge between them: it closes when someone steps on it. That makes a great burglar alarm!
Conductors let electricity through: metals like copper, steel and aluminium foil. Insulators do not: plastic, rubber, wood and paper. Wires are copper inside a coat of plastic.

Stay safe: use only small batteries. Never touch plugs or sockets: mains electricity is very dangerous. Never join a battery's two ends with just a wire: it gets hot. If anyone swallows a button battery, tell a grown-up at once.
Try it in the world: put a light switch next to a lamp and tap it: a switch powers the lamp it touches. For real: design a torch for someone, with a sketch of its circuit and its case.

exercises.hint: Follow the wire round with your finger. Is the loop complete, with a battery?
exercises.explain: True: the battery and the bulb are in a complete loop, so electricity flows round.

exercises.hint: Think of the path the electricity takes.
exercises.explain: A circuit is a complete loop that electricity flows round, from the battery and back.

exercises.prompt: Which of these lets electricity flow through it?
exercises.explain: The steel paper clip: it is metal, a conductor.

exercises.prompt: It is safe to play with plugs and sockets if you are careful.
exercises.hint: What does the lesson say about sockets?
exercises.explain: False: never touch plugs or sockets. Mains electricity is very dangerous.

exercises.prompt: Match each product to the part that makes it work.
exercises.hint: What does each product do: shine, spin or make a noise?
exercises.explain: A torch shines with a bulb or an LED, a fan spins with a motor, and an alarm sounds with a buzzer.

exercises.hint: Look at the switch: is it open or closed?
exercises.explain: False: the switch is open, so the loop is broken.

exercises.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?
exercises.hint: What happens to the loop when you switch off?
choices: opens and closes a gap in the loop
exercises.explain: A switch opens and closes a gap in the loop, so it turns the circuit off and on.
Conductors: copper, aluminium foil, steel. Insulators: plastic, rubber, wood.

exercises.prompt: Put designing a torch in order.
exercises.hint: Start with the design brief, and finish with the design cycle's last step.
items: write who it is for and what it must do
exercises.explain: Brief, drawing, circuit, case, then test and improve: the design cycle.

exercises.prompt: Which of these, put across the gap, would light the bulb?
exercises.hint: Which one is made of metal?
exercises.explain: A coin: it is metal, a conductor, so it closes the loop.

exercises.prompt: A pressure pad has two pieces of foil with sponge between them. What happens when someone steps on it?
exercises.hint: Foil is a metal. What happens when the two pieces meet?
choices: the foils touch and the loop is complete
exercises.explain: The foils are pressed together, so the gap closes, the loop is complete and the alarm sounds.

exercises.hint: Is the switch closed, and is there one complete loop?
exercises.explain: True: the switch is closed, so the loop is complete and both bulbs light, a little more dimly than one.

exercises.prompt: Your torch does not light. What should you check first?
exercises.hint: What does a bulb need to light?
choices: that the loop has no gaps and the battery works
exercises.explain: Check the loop for gaps or loose wires, then the battery: a bulb needs a complete loop and a working battery.

exercises.prompt: Why are wires coated in plastic?
choices: plastic is an insulator: safe to hold
exercises.explain: Plastic is an insulator, so the electricity stays in the copper and you can hold the wire safely.

exercises.prompt: Joining the two ends of a battery with just a wire is safe.
exercises.hint: What does the lesson say happens?
exercises.explain: False: with nothing else in the loop, the wire gets hot. Always put a bulb, buzzer or motor in the loop.

exercises.prompt: Sort the products by the part that makes them work.
exercises.hint: Does it shine, spin or make a sound?
exercises.explain: Shining: a torch and a night light use a bulb or an LED. Spinning: a fan and a toy car use a motor. Sounding: a doorbell and an alarm use a buzzer.

exercises.prompt: Order how a pressure-pad alarm works.
exercises.hint: Follow it from the foot to the sound.
exercises.explain: Someone steps on the pad, the two foils are pressed together, so the loop is complete, and electricity flows to the buzzer, which sounds.

exercises.prompt: A torch won't light. Match each fault to its fix.
exercises.hint: Each fault breaks the loop or stops the battery's push. What puts each right?
exercises.explain: A loose wire: join it again to close the loop. A flat battery: put in a new one. An open switch: close it. A broken bulb: put in a new bulb.
